title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI-generated outputs by injecting fabricated authoritative content into the data environment those systems draw from. The Hanover Institute did not exist as a genuine organisation, yet it produced a very large volume of policy-like text in a short time using a platform explicitly built to make content legible to AI systems. The failure this exposes is not a flaw in any single model but a vulnerability in how large language models treat apparent documentary evidence: text that resembles credible sourcing can shape responses regardless of whether the underlying institution is real.

The point of intervention was upstream of the model, at the level of training data or retrieval sources rather than at inference time. Catching it would have required source verification, meaning checks on whether a cited institution has verifiable existence, staff, and history, before that content influenced model outputs. No such check is established as standard practice in current AI data pipelines.

It is not established that the operation caused measurable changes in public opinion, that any AI company was aware of the content's origin, or that the Israeli government directed the operation with full knowledge of how it would be executed. Disclosure came through a foreign agent registration filing, not through a judicial finding, so the full chain of responsibility remains unresolved.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded fake think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for artificial intelligence systems like ChatGPT. The nonexistent institute, which has no physical address or named staff, presented pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including alleged war crimes, genocide claims, and Palestinian casualties. A New York media company called Piro Inc disclosed the operation to the US Justice Department under foreign agent registration laws, revealing it was part of a broader Israeli government campaign financed through tens of millions of dollars routed via European advertising firm Havas Media.

The campaign aimed to influence how chatbots present Israeli positions by seeding websites into training data used by AI systems. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the effort's effectiveness, with some calling it a waste of government money as American public support for Israel has declined significantly. Researchers noted that while the operation successfully shapes chatbot responses, it fails to change public opinion polling, which remains the Israeli government's actual concern. The broader campaign represents a new form of information manipulation where foreign governments and companies attempt to poison AI training data to influence automated responses.
